_**The Muppet Movie**_ is a 1979 musicalroadcomedy film, directed by James Frawley and produced by Jim Henson, and the first theatrical film to feature the Muppets. A co-production between the United Kingdom and the United States, the film was written by _The Muppet Show_ writers Jerry Juhl and Jack Burns. Produced during the third season of _The Muppet Show_, the film tells the origin story of the Muppets, as Kermit the Frog embarks on a cross-country trip to Los Angeles, encountering several of the Muppets—who all share the same ambition of finding success in professional show business—along the way while being pursued by Doc Hopper, a greedy restaurateur with intentions of recruiting Kermit to promote his frog legs business.
The film stars Muppet performers Henson, Frank Oz, Jerry Nelson, Richard Hunt, and Dave Goelz, as well as Charles Durning and Austin Pendleton, and it features cameo appearances by Bob Hope, Dom DeLuise, James Coburn, Cloris Leachman, Richard Pryor, Telly Savalas, Edgar Bergen (in his final film appearance before his death), Orson Welles, Madeline Kahn, Milton Berle, Carol Kane, Steve Martin, Mel Brooks, Elliott Gould, and Paul Williams. Notable for its surreal humour, meta-references and prolific use of cameos, _The Muppet Movie_ was released by Associated Film Distribution in the United Kingdom on May 31, 1979, and in the United States on June 22, 1979.
The film received critical praise, including two Academy Award nominations for Paul Williams and Kenneth Ascher's musical score and their song "Rainbow Connection". The film grossed $76.7 million worldwide against an $8 million budget. _The Muppet Movie_ was followed by seven feature films starring the Muppets as well as several more television series and media. In 2009, the film was deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" by the Library of Congress and selected for preservation in the National Film Registry.

The story opens with the Muppets sitting down for a private screening of a movie that acts as an origin story of how they all met.
Kermit the Frog lives a simple life in a Florida swamp. After he plays his banjo and sings "Rainbow Connection", he is approached by Bernie, a talent agent who encourages him to pursue a career in show business. Inspired, Kermit sets off on a cross-country trip to Hollywood.
He meets Fozzie Bear, who is working as a hapless stand-up comedian, and invites him on his journey. The two set out in Fozzie's 1951 Studebaker but are pursued by entrepreneur Doc Hopper and his assistant Max, who try to convince Kermit to be the new spokesfrog of Hopper's struggling French-friedfrog legs restaurant franchise. Horrified, Kermit refuses, and he and Fozzie drive away. Unwilling to accept Kermit's refusal, Hopper follows the pair and resorts to increasingly forceful means of persuasion. In an old church, Kermit and Fozzie meet the rock band Dr. Teeth and the Electric Mayhem, and their manager Scooter, who help them disguise their car. Driving on, they meet and are joined by Gonzo and his girlfriend Camilla the Chicken, who are also interested in becoming movie stars. They trade in their failing vehicle at a used car lot, where they meet Sweetums. They invite Sweetums to come with them, but he runs away. The others drive away, only for Sweetums to emerge and reveal that he had only gone to pack his things.
The group meets Miss Piggy at a county fair and she and Kermit become love-stricken with each other. When they meet for dinner that night, Hopper and Max abduct Miss Piggy as bait to lure Kermit. When they capture Kermit, Hopper orders mad scientist Professor Krassman to give Kermit an electric lobotomy so that he would willingly perform in Hopper's advertisements, but Miss Piggy knocks out Hopper's henchmen and causes Krassman to have his brain fried by his own device. Immediately after the fight, however, Miss Piggy receives a job offer and abandons a devastated Kermit.

Joined by Rowlf the Dog, the Muppets pick up Miss Piggy – who is hitchhiking on the side of the road – and continue their journey; but their car breaks down in the desert. Sitting at a campfire, the group realizes that they will likely miss the auditions the next day. Kermit wanders off, ashamed for bringing his friends on a fruitless journey, but personal reflection restores his commitment. He returns to camp, where he discovers that the Electric Mayhem have come to their rescue, having learned of their plight by reading ahead in the film's script. The Mayhem offer to drive the group the rest of the way in their bus.
The group is warned by a reformed Max that Hopper has hired an assassin, Snake Walker, to kill Kermit. Kermit decides to face his aggressor and proposes a Western-style showdown in a nearby ghost town. There, they find inventor Dr. Bunsen Honeydew and his assistant Beaker. Kermit and his friends are saved when one of Dr. Honeydew's inventions, "insta-grow" pills, enlarges Mayhem drummer Animal, who frightens away Hopper and his henchmen.
Once the Muppets reach the Hollywood studio, they meet executive Lew Lord, who signs them to a "standard 'rich and famous' contract". The first take in their attempt to perform the script goes awry when Gonzo crashes into the prop rainbow, which knocks the scenery down and an explosion blows a hole in the roof of the studio, but a real rainbow shines through the hole and illuminates all the Muppets. Joined by characters from other Henson productions – including _Sesame Street_, _[Emmet Otter's Jug-Band Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmet\_Otter's\_Jug-Band\_Christmas "Emmet Otter's Jug-Band Christmas")_, and _The Land of Gorch_ – the Muppets sing the final verse in a reprise of "Rainbow Connection". As the film ends, Sweetums tears through the screen, elated that he caught up with them.

*   Charles Durning as Doc Hopper, a businessman, entrepreneur, and restaurateur.  
*   Austin Pendleton as Max, Doc Hopper's shy right-hand man and sidekick.  
*   Scott Walker as Snake Walker, an assassin who specializes in killing frogs.  
*   H.B. Haggerty as Lumberjack  
*   Bruce Kirby as Gate Guard  
*   James Frawley as a Waiter at El Sleezo Café where Fozzie is doing his act

*   Jim Henson as Kermit the Frog, Rowlf the Dog, Dr. Teeth, Waldorf and The Swedish Chef  
*   Frank Oz as Miss Piggy, Fozzie Bear, Animal, Sam Eagle and Marvin Suggs  
*   Jerry Nelson as Floyd Pepper, Crazy Harry, Robin the Frog, Lew Zealand and Camilla the Chicken  
*   Richard Hunt as Scooter, Statler, Janice, Sweetums and Beaker  
*   Dave Goelz as The Great Gonzo, Zoot, Dr. Bunsen Honeydew and Doglion  
*   Caroll Spinney as Big Bird
Oz appears in a cameo as a biker who beats up Fozzie Bear[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:22-10) while Steve Whitmire appears as a man in the Bogen County Fair.

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
[edit]
*   Dom DeLuise as Bernie, a Hollywood agent who meets Kermit in the swamp. The character's name alludes to Bernie Brillstein, talent agent and producer of the original _Muppet Show_.  
*   James Coburn as the El Sleezo Café Owner  
*   Madeline Kahn as an El Sleezo Patron with the same rhotacism and personality Kahn used for Lili von Shtupp in _Blazing Saddles_  
*   Telly Savalas as El Sleezo Tough  
*   Carol Kane as the lisping "miss" (summoned by the word “myth”)  
*   Paul Williams as the El Sleezo Pianist.  
*   Milton Berle as Mad Man Mooney, a used car salesman who employs Sweetums as a jack.  
*   Elliott Gould as the Compère who announces Miss Piggy as the winner of the Bogen County Beauty Pageant.  
*   Edgar Bergen as himself and Charlie McCarthy playing judges at the County Fair. This appearance marks Bergen's last film; he died soon after. The film was dedicated in his memory.  
*   Bob Hope as an Ice Cream Vendor serving cones to Fozzie at the County Fair.  
*   Richard Pryor as a Balloon Vendor selling balloons to Gonzo at the County Fair.  
*   Steve Martin as an insolent waiter working at the restaurant where Rowlf plays piano.  
*   Mel Brooks as Professor Krassman, a mad scientist hired by Doc Hopper.  
*   Cloris Leachman as Miss Tracy, Lew Lord's secretary who is allergic to animals.  
*   Orson Welles as Lew Lord, a Hollywood producer and studio executive. The character's name alludes to Sir Lew Grade, head of ATV, the British company that co-produced _The Muppet Show_.

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
After the popularity of the Muppets had grown following the success of _The Muppet Show_, Lew Grade agreed to finance the production of the film and signed the deal with his company ITC Entertainment,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199472-11) which helped Jim Henson finance the film.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-12) After the film's production greenlit, Jim Henson and selected team members traveled to California various times to develop the script, music, and infrastructure in Hollywood to shoot the film.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:6-13)James Frawley was hired to direct the movie due to the film's challenges.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:6-13)

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
During Frawley and Henson's first meeting in London, they were concerned that the Muppets would not blend well in real life.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-Frawley-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:5-15) Along with Frank Oz and the team, they filmed and tested how the characters would appear in real-world locations during the first few days of June 1978 in a UK meadow.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:6-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-Frawley-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:5-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:1-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199473-17) During filming tests, a cow was ambled near Fozzie for an unexpected rear look at a comparison between fake and natural fur hair.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199473-17) The camera tests attracted the investment of ITC Entertainment.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:6-13) On July 3, 1978, Henson flew to Los Angeles again to begin shooting for the film.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:1-16)

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
In order for Kermit to ride a bicycle in a full-body shot, a Kermit puppet with legs was posed onto the seat and his legs and arms were attached to the pedals and handlebars. An overhead crane with a marionette system held the bicycle through strong strings invisible to the camera, guiding the bicycle forward.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-27) The crane and system were out of the camera's frame of vision.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-Frawley-14) Specially made, remote-controlled puppets were placed on the set and controlled by puppeteers out of the frame. A dancing Kermit and Fozzie Bear were operated by Henson and Oz in front of a blue screen, and they were composited onto a separate reel of the stage._[citation needed_] For scenes involving Fozzie driving a Studebaker, cables, TV monitors, puppeteers, and its Muppets were filled in.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199473%E2%80%9374-28) A dwarf would sit in the trunk and control via remote control. A television monitor showed what was ahead.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199474-29)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:22-10)

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
The closing reprise of "Rainbow Connection" featured a crowd of more than 250 Muppet characters—virtually every Muppet that had been created up to that point in time.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:22-10)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:5-15)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:3-30) According to Henson Archivist Karen Falk, 137 puppeteers were enlisted from the Puppeteers of America (along with the regular Muppets performers) to perform every Muppet extant.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:22-10)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:3-30) Prior to the day-long filming of the shot, Henson gave the enthusiastic participants a lesson in the art of cinematic puppetry. The scene involved 150 puppeteers performing in a pit that was 6 feet (1.8 m) deep and 17 feet (5.2 m) wide.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:22-10)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:3-30) In September 1978, Edgar Bergen, Henson's idol who appeared in a cameo role, died shortly after completing his scenes. Henson was asked by his family to say a few words with Kermit for his memorial service. Henson agreed, and he attended Bergen's memorial service for its speech.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199475-31) Henson dedicated the film to his memory.

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
The film's music and lyrics were written by Paul Williams and Kenneth Ascher. Regarding the music's composition, Williams said; "Jim Henson gave you more [creative] freedom than anybody I've ever worked with in my life. I said, 'You want to hear the songs as we're writing them?' He said, 'No. I'll hear them in the studio. I know I'm gonna love them.' You just don't get that kind of freedom on a project these days."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-songfacts-32) "Never Before, Never Again" was originally sung by Johnny Mathis, but was changed to Miss Piggy when Jim Henson thought it would be funnier if she sang it to herself.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:3-30) Mathis would later sing the song in the television special _The Muppets Go Hollywood_.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:3-30)
"Movin' Right Along", "Never Before, Never Again", and "I Hope That Somethin' Better Comes Along" were shortened in the film, compared to their soundtrack versions, for continuity purposes._[citation needed_] The latter, a duet between Rowlf and Kermit, contained references that the studio considered too mature for children, although the song appeared complete in the British theatrical and home video debut versions._[citation needed_]

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
_The Muppet Movie_ had a royal premiere at the Leicester Square Theatre in London on May 31, 1979, attended by Princess Anne.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-33)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199474-29) In the United States, the film premiered with a celebration at the Coconut Grove in Hollywood, Los Angeles.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199474-29)_[when?_] It was later released with limited release in New York City,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-Muppet_Movie_North_American_Debuts-34)Toronto,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-35)Los Angeles,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-Muppet_Movie_North_American_Debuts-34)Wichita,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-36)Kansas City,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-37)Austin,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-Muppet_Movie_Austin-38) and the Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-39) on June 22, 1979.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-Muppet_Movie_North_American_Debuts-34) The film rolled out gradually throughout the United States and Canada.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-40) In celebration of the film's 40th anniversary, _The Muppet Movie_ returned to theaters for two days on July 25 and 30,

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
In its first six days at the Leicester Square Theatre, it grossed $31,884.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-50) The film would later earn over $76.7 million in the United States and Canada,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJay_Jones2013296-7) returning $32 million in box office rentals.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-51)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-52) For 32 years, _The Muppet Movie_ was the highest-grossing puppet film until the release of _The Muppets_ in 2011.
The film's successful theatrical release encouraged Lew Grade into furthering his own film distribution company, which later backfired with the massive box office failures of _[Can't Stop the Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Can't\_Stop\_the\_Music "Can't Stop the Music")_ (from EMI) and _Raise the Titanic_ (from ITC), both released by Associated Film Distribution just a year later.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-grade-53)
_The Muppet Movie_ currently holds an 89% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 102 reviews. The site's consensus says "_The Muppet Movie_, the big-screen debut of Jim Henson's plush creations, is smart, lighthearted, and fun for all ages."[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-RT-54) On Metacritic, the film has a weighted average score of 74 out of 100 based on 7 reviews, indicating "generally favorable reviews".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-55)

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
The film received highly positive reviews in the United States. Roger Ebert of the _Chicago Sun-Times_ gave the film three-and-a-half out of four stars. In his favorable review, he was fascinated that "_The Muppet Movie_ not only stars the Muppets but, for the first time, shows us their feet."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-ebert-56)Vincent Canby of _The New York Times_ offered equal praise, stating that the film "demonstrates once again that there's always room in movies for unbridled amiability when it is governed by intelligence and wit."[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-57)Gene Siskel of the _Chicago Tribune_ gave the film three-and-a-half stars out of four and called it "surely one of the summer's most entertaining films," which "does a fairly nice job of trying to be all things to all people. Which is not an easy job."[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-58)Dale Pollock of _Variety_ wrote, "'The Muppet Movie' is a winner... Script by Jerry Juhl and Jack Burns incorporates the zingy one-liners and bad puns that have become the teleseries' trade mark, but also develops the Muppets themselves as thinking, feeling characters."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-59) Kathleen Carroll of the _New York Daily News_ wrote that "with the exception of Brooks' wacky scene and Steve Martin's funny bit as a snooty waiter, the cameo appearances by such stars as Bob Hope and Richard Pryor tend to slow the action down just as the bland musical numbers by Paul Williams and Kenny Asher interrupt the flow of the movie.

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
Still _The Muppet Movie_ should entrance both young and old as the Muppets further endear themselves with their crazy antics, their playful puns and their very human characteristics."[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-60)Rex Reed, in the same newspaper, reacted more enthusiastically to the film, remarking that "if there's any doubt, _The Muppet Movie_ will make believers and fans out of the worst pessimists. These lovable characters are so real and so endearing that I was never aware of the human hands making them work from mysterious hiding places. The Muppets made a wide-eyed, child out of me, and I hope they continue to do so until I'm in my wheelchair."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-61)

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
Charles Champlin of the _Los Angeles Times_ wrote, "as you might well expect, it is hip, funny, technically ingenious, fast-moving, melodious, richly produced, contemporary and equally and utterly beguiling to grown-ups and small persons."[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-62) Katrine Ames of _Newsweek_ stated, "'The Muppet Movie' is a delectable grab bag of influences — stories by L. Frank Baum and Lewis Carroll, Westerns, the [Crosby-Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_to_... "Road to ...") and Garland-Rooney movies — as well as its own inventive devices. The result is a kind of '[That's Entertainment!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That's_Entertainment! "That's Entertainment!")' with a plot attached. Its charm — and success — lie primarily in its loving pokes at Hollywood conventions and in the lovable characters who do the poking."[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-63) John Skow of _Time_ magazine offered a more mixed response, saying that "the transition from the yank-'em-off-if-they-bomb lunacy of the TV show to the coherent narration of the film is not a complete success. Muppet magic remains a bewildering succession of wonderful bits, and perhaps the movie's best occurs when Rowlf the Dog, who is a barroom pianist, commiserates with Kermit, who has just been deserted by Miss Piggy. The two sing a nice, rueful song about women—the can't-live-with-them, can't-live-without-them kind of thing."[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-64)

texts.1:
| Box office | $76.7 million[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-9) |
_**The Muppet Movie**_ is a 1979 musicalroadcomedy film, directed by James Frawley and produced by Jim Henson, and the first theatrical film to feature the Muppets. A co-production between the United Kingdom and the United States, the film was written by _The Muppet Show_ writers Jerry Juhl and Jack Burns. Produced during the third season of _The Muppet Show_, the film tells the origin story of the Muppets, as Kermit the Frog embarks on a cross-country trip to Los Angeles, encountering several of the Muppets—who all share the same ambition of finding success in professional show business—along the way while being pursued by Doc Hopper, a greedy restaurateur with intentions of recruiting Kermit to promote his frog legs business.
The film stars Muppet performers Henson, Frank Oz, Jerry Nelson, Richard Hunt, and Dave Goelz, as well as Charles Durning and Austin Pendleton, and it features cameo appearances by Bob Hope, Dom DeLuise, James Coburn, Cloris Leachman, Richard Pryor, Telly Savalas, Edgar Bergen (in his final film appearance before his death), Orson Welles, Madeline Kahn, Milton Berle, Carol Kane, Steve Martin, Mel Brooks, Elliott Gould, and Paul Williams. Notable for its surreal humour, meta-references and prolific use of cameos, _The Muppet Movie_ was released by Associated Film Distribution in the United Kingdom on May 31, 1979, and in the United States on June 22, 1979.
The film received critical praise, including two Academy Award nominations for Paul Williams and Kenneth Ascher's musical score and their song "Rainbow Connection". The film grossed $76.7 million worldwide against an $8 million budget. _The Muppet Movie_ was followed by seven feature films starring the Muppets as well as several more television series and media. In 2009, the film was deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" by the Library of Congress and selected for preservation in the National Film Registry.
texts.2:
The story opens with the Muppets sitting down for a private screening of a movie that acts as an origin story of how they all met.
Kermit the Frog lives a simple life in a Florida swamp. After he plays his banjo and sings "Rainbow Connection", he is approached by Bernie, a talent agent who encourages him to pursue a career in show business. Inspired, Kermit sets off on a cross-country trip to Hollywood.
He meets Fozzie Bear, who is working as a hapless stand-up comedian, and invites him on his journey. The two set out in Fozzie's 1951 Studebaker but are pursued by entrepreneur Doc Hopper and his assistant Max, who try to convince Kermit to be the new spokesfrog of Hopper's struggling French-friedfrog legs restaurant franchise. Horrified, Kermit refuses, and he and Fozzie drive away. Unwilling to accept Kermit's refusal, Hopper follows the pair and resorts to increasingly forceful means of persuasion. In an old church, Kermit and Fozzie meet the rock band Dr. Teeth and the Electric Mayhem, and their manager Scooter, who help them disguise their car. Driving on, they meet and are joined by Gonzo and his girlfriend Camilla the Chicken, who are also interested in becoming movie stars. They trade in their failing vehicle at a used car lot, where they meet Sweetums. They invite Sweetums to come with them, but he runs away. The others drive away, only for Sweetums to emerge and reveal that he had only gone to pack his things.
The group meets Miss Piggy at a county fair and she and Kermit become love-stricken with each other. When they meet for dinner that night, Hopper and Max abduct Miss Piggy as bait to lure Kermit. When they capture Kermit, Hopper orders mad scientist Professor Krassman to give Kermit an electric lobotomy so that he would willingly perform in Hopper's advertisements, but Miss Piggy knocks out Hopper's henchmen and causes Krassman to have his brain fried by his own device. Immediately after the fight, however, Miss Piggy receives a job offer and abandons a devastated Kermit.
texts.3:
Joined by Rowlf the Dog, the Muppets pick up Miss Piggy – who is hitchhiking on the side of the road – and continue their journey; but their car breaks down in the desert. Sitting at a campfire, the group realizes that they will likely miss the auditions the next day. Kermit wanders off, ashamed for bringing his friends on a fruitless journey, but personal reflection restores his commitment. He returns to camp, where he discovers that the Electric Mayhem have come to their rescue, having learned of their plight by reading ahead in the film's script. The Mayhem offer to drive the group the rest of the way in their bus.
The group is warned by a reformed Max that Hopper has hired an assassin, Snake Walker, to kill Kermit. Kermit decides to face his aggressor and proposes a Western-style showdown in a nearby ghost town. There, they find inventor Dr. Bunsen Honeydew and his assistant Beaker. Kermit and his friends are saved when one of Dr. Honeydew's inventions, "insta-grow" pills, enlarges Mayhem drummer Animal, who frightens away Hopper and his henchmen.
Once the Muppets reach the Hollywood studio, they meet executive Lew Lord, who signs them to a "standard 'rich and famous' contract". The first take in their attempt to perform the script goes awry when Gonzo crashes into the prop rainbow, which knocks the scenery down and an explosion blows a hole in the roof of the studio, but a real rainbow shines through the hole and illuminates all the Muppets. Joined by characters from other Henson productions – including _Sesame Street_, _[Emmet Otter's Jug-Band Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmet\_Otter's\_Jug-Band\_Christmas "Emmet Otter's Jug-Band Christmas")_, and _The Land of Gorch_ – the Muppets sing the final verse in a reprise of "Rainbow Connection". As the film ends, Sweetums tears through the screen, elated that he caught up with them.

texts.5:
### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
[edit]
*   Dom DeLuise as Bernie, a Hollywood agent who meets Kermit in the swamp. The character's name alludes to Bernie Brillstein, talent agent and producer of the original _Muppet Show_.  
*   James Coburn as the El Sleezo Café Owner  
*   Madeline Kahn as an El Sleezo Patron with the same rhotacism and personality Kahn used for Lili von Shtupp in _Blazing Saddles_  
*   Telly Savalas as El Sleezo Tough  
*   Carol Kane as the lisping "miss" (summoned by the word “myth”)  
*   Paul Williams as the El Sleezo Pianist.  
*   Milton Berle as Mad Man Mooney, a used car salesman who employs Sweetums as a jack.  
*   Elliott Gould as the Compère who announces Miss Piggy as the winner of the Bogen County Beauty Pageant.  
*   Edgar Bergen as himself and Charlie McCarthy playing judges at the County Fair. This appearance marks Bergen's last film; he died soon after. The film was dedicated in his memory.  
*   Bob Hope as an Ice Cream Vendor serving cones to Fozzie at the County Fair.  
*   Richard Pryor as a Balloon Vendor selling balloons to Gonzo at the County Fair.  
*   Steve Martin as an insolent waiter working at the restaurant where Rowlf plays piano.  
*   Mel Brooks as Professor Krassman, a mad scientist hired by Doc Hopper.  
*   Cloris Leachman as Miss Tracy, Lew Lord's secretary who is allergic to animals.  
*   Orson Welles as Lew Lord, a Hollywood producer and studio executive. The character's name alludes to Sir Lew Grade, head of ATV, the British company that co-produced _The Muppet Show_.
texts.6:
### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
After the popularity of the Muppets had grown following the success of _The Muppet Show_, Lew Grade agreed to finance the production of the film and signed the deal with his company ITC Entertainment,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199472-11) which helped Jim Henson finance the film.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-12) After the film's production greenlit, Jim Henson and selected team members traveled to California various times to develop the script, music, and infrastructure in Hollywood to shoot the film.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:6-13)James Frawley was hired to direct the movie due to the film's challenges.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:6-13)
texts.7:
### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
During Frawley and Henson's first meeting in London, they were concerned that the Muppets would not blend well in real life.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-Frawley-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:5-15) Along with Frank Oz and the team, they filmed and tested how the characters would appear in real-world locations during the first few days of June 1978 in a UK meadow.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:6-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-Frawley-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:5-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:1-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199473-17) During filming tests, a cow was ambled near Fozzie for an unexpected rear look at a comparison between fake and natural fur hair.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199473-17) The camera tests attracted the investment of ITC Entertainment.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:6-13) On July 3, 1978, Henson flew to Los Angeles again to begin shooting for the film.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:1-16)
texts.10:
### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
In order for Kermit to ride a bicycle in a full-body shot, a Kermit puppet with legs was posed onto the seat and his legs and arms were attached to the pedals and handlebars. An overhead crane with a marionette system held the bicycle through strong strings invisible to the camera, guiding the bicycle forward.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-27) The crane and system were out of the camera's frame of vision.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-Frawley-14) Specially made, remote-controlled puppets were placed on the set and controlled by puppeteers out of the frame. A dancing Kermit and Fozzie Bear were operated by Henson and Oz in front of a blue screen, and they were composited onto a separate reel of the stage._[citation needed_] For scenes involving Fozzie driving a Studebaker, cables, TV monitors, puppeteers, and its Muppets were filled in.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199473%E2%80%9374-28) A dwarf would sit in the trunk and control via remote control. A television monitor showed what was ahead.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199474-29)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:22-10)
texts.11:
### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
The closing reprise of "Rainbow Connection" featured a crowd of more than 250 Muppet characters—virtually every Muppet that had been created up to that point in time.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:22-10)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:5-15)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:3-30) According to Henson Archivist Karen Falk, 137 puppeteers were enlisted from the Puppeteers of America (along with the regular Muppets performers) to perform every Muppet extant.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:22-10)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:3-30) Prior to the day-long filming of the shot, Henson gave the enthusiastic participants a lesson in the art of cinematic puppetry. The scene involved 150 puppeteers performing in a pit that was 6 feet (1.8 m) deep and 17 feet (5.2 m) wide.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:22-10)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:3-30) In September 1978, Edgar Bergen, Henson's idol who appeared in a cameo role, died shortly after completing his scenes. Henson was asked by his family to say a few words with Kermit for his memorial service. Henson agreed, and he attended Bergen's memorial service for its speech.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199475-31) Henson dedicated the film to his memory.
texts.12:
### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
The film's music and lyrics were written by Paul Williams and Kenneth Ascher. Regarding the music's composition, Williams said; "Jim Henson gave you more [creative] freedom than anybody I've ever worked with in my life. I said, 'You want to hear the songs as we're writing them?' He said, 'No. I'll hear them in the studio. I know I'm gonna love them.' You just don't get that kind of freedom on a project these days."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-songfacts-32) "Never Before, Never Again" was originally sung by Johnny Mathis, but was changed to Miss Piggy when Jim Henson thought it would be funnier if she sang it to herself.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:3-30) Mathis would later sing the song in the television special _The Muppets Go Hollywood_.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-:3-30)
"Movin' Right Along", "Never Before, Never Again", and "I Hope That Somethin' Better Comes Along" were shortened in the film, compared to their soundtrack versions, for continuity purposes._[citation needed_] The latter, a duet between Rowlf and Kermit, contained references that the studio considered too mature for children, although the song appeared complete in the British theatrical and home video debut versions._[citation needed_]
texts.13:
### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
_The Muppet Movie_ had a royal premiere at the Leicester Square Theatre in London on May 31, 1979, attended by Princess Anne.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-33)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199474-29) In the United States, the film premiered with a celebration at the Coconut Grove in Hollywood, Los Angeles.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199474-29)_[when?_] It was later released with limited release in New York City,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-Muppet_Movie_North_American_Debuts-34)Toronto,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-35)Los Angeles,[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-Muppet_Movie_North_American_Debuts-34)Wichita,[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-36)Kansas City,[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-37)Austin,[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-Muppet_Movie_Austin-38) and the Dallas–Fort Worth metroplex[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-39) on June 22, 1979.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-Muppet_Movie_North_American_Debuts-34) The film rolled out gradually throughout the United States and Canada.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-40) In celebration of the film's 40th anniversary, _The Muppet Movie_ returned to theaters for two days on July 25 and 30,
texts.16:
### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
In its first six days at the Leicester Square Theatre, it grossed $31,884.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-50) The film would later earn over $76.7 million in the United States and Canada,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-FOOTNOTEJay_Jones2013296-7) returning $32 million in box office rentals.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-51)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-52) For 32 years, _The Muppet Movie_ was the highest-grossing puppet film until the release of _The Muppets_ in 2011.
The film's successful theatrical release encouraged Lew Grade into furthering his own film distribution company, which later backfired with the massive box office failures of _[Can't Stop the Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Can't\_Stop\_the\_Music "Can't Stop the Music")_ (from EMI) and _Raise the Titanic_ (from ITC), both released by Associated Film Distribution just a year later.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-grade-53)
_The Muppet Movie_ currently holds an 89% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes, based on 102 reviews. The site's consensus says "_The Muppet Movie_, the big-screen debut of Jim Henson's plush creations, is smart, lighthearted, and fun for all ages."[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-RT-54) On Metacritic, the film has a weighted average score of 74 out of 100 based on 7 reviews, indicating "generally favorable reviews".[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-55)
texts.17:
### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
The film received highly positive reviews in the United States. Roger Ebert of the _Chicago Sun-Times_ gave the film three-and-a-half out of four stars. In his favorable review, he was fascinated that "_The Muppet Movie_ not only stars the Muppets but, for the first time, shows us their feet."[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-ebert-56)Vincent Canby of _The New York Times_ offered equal praise, stating that the film "demonstrates once again that there's always room in movies for unbridled amiability when it is governed by intelligence and wit."[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-57)Gene Siskel of the _Chicago Tribune_ gave the film three-and-a-half stars out of four and called it "surely one of the summer's most entertaining films," which "does a fairly nice job of trying to be all things to all people. Which is not an easy job."[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-58)Dale Pollock of _Variety_ wrote, "'The Muppet Movie' is a winner... Script by Jerry Juhl and Jack Burns incorporates the zingy one-liners and bad puns that have become the teleseries' trade mark, but also develops the Muppets themselves as thinking, feeling characters."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-59) Kathleen Carroll of the _New York Daily News_ wrote that "with the exception of Brooks' wacky scene and Steve Martin's funny bit as a snooty waiter, the cameo appearances by such stars as Bob Hope and Richard Pryor tend to slow the action down just as the bland musical numbers by Paul Williams and Kenny Asher interrupt the flow of the movie.
texts.18:
### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
Still _The Muppet Movie_ should entrance both young and old as the Muppets further endear themselves with their crazy antics, their playful puns and their very human characteristics."[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-60)Rex Reed, in the same newspaper, reacted more enthusiastically to the film, remarking that "if there's any doubt, _The Muppet Movie_ will make believers and fans out of the worst pessimists. These lovable characters are so real and so endearing that I was never aware of the human hands making them work from mysterious hiding places. The Muppets made a wide-eyed, child out of me, and I hope they continue to do so until I'm in my wheelchair."[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-61)
texts.19:
### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
Charles Champlin of the _Los Angeles Times_ wrote, "as you might well expect, it is hip, funny, technically ingenious, fast-moving, melodious, richly produced, contemporary and equally and utterly beguiling to grown-ups and small persons."[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-62) Katrine Ames of _Newsweek_ stated, "'The Muppet Movie' is a delectable grab bag of influences — stories by L. Frank Baum and Lewis Carroll, Westerns, the [Crosby-Hope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_to_... "Road to ...") and Garland-Rooney movies — as well as its own inventive devices. The result is a kind of '[That's Entertainment!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/That's_Entertainment! "That's Entertainment!")' with a plot attached. Its charm — and success — lie primarily in its loving pokes at Hollywood conventions and in the lovable characters who do the poking."[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-63) John Skow of _Time_ magazine offered a more mixed response, saying that "the transition from the yank-'em-off-if-they-bomb lunacy of the TV show to the coherent narration of the film is not a complete success. Muppet magic remains a bewildering succession of wonderful bits, and perhaps the movie's best occurs when Rowlf the Dog, who is a barroom pianist, commiserates with Kermit, who has just been deserted by Miss Piggy. The two sing a nice, rueful song about women—the can't-live-with-them, can't-live-without-them kind of thing."[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Muppet_Movie#cite_note-64)

Title: The Muppet Movie
Chunks: 3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10,24,25,26,27,28
The film stars Muppet performers Henson, Frank Oz, Jerry Nelson, Richard Hunt, and Dave Goelz, as well as Charles Durning and Austin Pendleton, and it features cameo appearances by Bob Hope, Dom DeLuise, James Coburn, Cloris Leachman, Richard Pryor, Telly Savalas, Edgar Bergen (in his final film appearance before his death), Orson Welles, Madeline Kahn, Milton Berle, Carol Kane, Steve Martin, Mel Brooks, Elliott Gould, and Paul Williams. Notable for its surreal humour, meta-references and prolific use of cameos, _The Muppet Movie_ was released by Associated Film Distribution in the United Kingdom on May 31, 1979, and in the United States on June 22, 1979.
The film received critical praise, including two Academy Award nominations for Paul Williams and Kenneth Ascher's musical score and their song "Rainbow Connection". The film grossed $76.7 million worldwide against an $8 million budget. _The Muppet Movie_ was followed by seven feature films starring the Muppets as well as several more television series and media. In 2009, the film was deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" by the Library of Congress and selected for preservation in the National Film Registry.
The story opens with the Muppets sitting down for a private screening of a movie that acts as an origin story of how they all met.
Kermit the Frog lives a simple life in a Florida swamp. After he plays his banjo and sings "Rainbow Connection", he is approached by Bernie, a talent agent who encourages him to pursue a career in show business. Inspired, Kermit sets off on a cross-country trip to Hollywood.

He meets Fozzie Bear, who is working as a hapless stand-up comedian, and invites him on his journey. The two set out in Fozzie's 1951 Studebaker but are pursued by entrepreneur Doc Hopper and his assistant Max, who try to convince Kermit to be the new spokesfrog of Hopper's struggling French-friedfrog legs restaurant franchise. Horrified, Kermit refuses, and he and Fozzie drive away. Unwilling to accept Kermit's refusal, Hopper follows the pair and resorts to increasingly forceful means of persuasion. In an old church, Kermit and Fozzie meet the rock band Dr. Teeth and the Electric Mayhem, and their manager Scooter, who help them disguise their car. Driving on, they meet and are joined by Gonzo and his girlfriend Camilla the Chicken, who are also interested in becoming movie stars. They trade in their failing vehicle at a used car lot, where they meet Sweetums. They invite Sweetums to come with them, but he runs away. The others drive away, only for Sweetums to emerge and reveal that he had only gone to pack his things.
The group meets Miss Piggy at a county fair and she and Kermit become love-stricken with each other. When they meet for dinner that night, Hopper and Max abduct Miss Piggy as bait to lure Kermit. When they capture Kermit, Hopper orders mad scientist Professor Krassman to give Kermit an electric lobotomy so that he would willingly perform in Hopper's advertisements, but Miss Piggy knocks out Hopper's henchmen and causes Krassman to have his brain fried by his own device. Immediately after the fight, however, Miss Piggy receives a job offer and abandons a devastated Kermit.

Joined by Rowlf the Dog, the Muppets pick up Miss Piggy – who is hitchhiking on the side of the road – and continue their journey; but their car breaks down in the desert. Sitting at a campfire, the group realizes that they will likely miss the auditions the next day. Kermit wanders off, ashamed for bringing his friends on a fruitless journey, but personal reflection restores his commitment. He returns to camp, where he discovers that the Electric Mayhem have come to their rescue, having learned of their plight by reading ahead in the film's script. The Mayhem offer to drive the group the rest of the way in their bus.
The group is warned by a reformed Max that Hopper has hired an assassin, Snake Walker, to kill Kermit. Kermit decides to face his aggressor and proposes a Western-style showdown in a nearby ghost town. There, they find inventor Dr. Bunsen Honeydew and his assistant Beaker. Kermit and his friends are saved when one of Dr. Honeydew's inventions, "insta-grow" pills, enlarges Mayhem drummer Animal, who frightens away Hopper and his henchmen.
Once the Muppets reach the Hollywood studio, they meet executive Lew Lord, who signs them to a "standard 'rich and famous' contract". The first take in their attempt to perform the script goes awry when Gonzo crashes into the prop rainbow, which knocks the scenery down and an explosion blows a hole in the roof of the studio, but a real rainbow shines through the hole and illuminates all the Muppets. Joined by characters from other Henson productions – including _Sesame Street_, _[Emmet Otter's Jug-Band Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmet\_Otter's\_Jug-Band\_Christmas "Emmet Otter's Jug-Band Christmas")_, and _The Land of Gorch_ – the Muppets sing the final verse in a reprise of "Rainbow Connection". As the film ends, Sweetums tears through the screen, elated that he caught up with them.

*   Charles Durning as Doc Hopper, a businessman, entrepreneur, and restaurateur.  
*   Austin Pendleton as Max, Doc Hopper's shy right-hand man and sidekick.  
*   Scott Walker as Snake Walker, an assassin who specializes in killing frogs.  
*   H.B. Haggerty as Lumberjack  
*   Bruce Kirby as Gate Guard  
*   James Frawley as a Waiter at El Sleezo Café where Fozzie is doing his act

*   Jim Henson as Kermit the Frog, Rowlf the Dog, Dr. Teeth, Waldorf and The Swedish Chef  
*   Frank Oz as Miss Piggy, Fozzie Bear, Animal, Sam Eagle and Marvin Suggs  
*   Jerry Nelson as Floyd Pepper, Crazy Harry, Robin the Frog, Lew Zealand and Camilla the Chicken  
*   Richard Hunt as Scooter, Statler, Janice, Sweetums and Beaker  
*   Dave Goelz as The Great Gonzo, Zoot, Dr. Bunsen Honeydew and Doglion  
*   Caroll Spinney as Big Bird
Oz appears in a cameo as a biker who beats up Fozzie Bear[[9]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-:22-10) while Steve Whitmire appears as a man in the Bogen County Fair.

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
[edit]
*   Dom DeLuise as Bernie, a Hollywood agent who meets Kermit in the swamp. The character's name alludes to Bernie Brillstein, talent agent and producer of the original _Muppet Show_.  
*   James Coburn as the El Sleezo Café Owner  
*   Madeline Kahn as an El Sleezo Patron with the same rhotacism and personality Kahn used for Lili von Shtupp in _Blazing Saddles_  
*   Telly Savalas as El Sleezo Tough  
*   Carol Kane as the lisping "miss" (summoned by the word “myth”)  
*   Paul Williams as the El Sleezo Pianist.  
*   Milton Berle as Mad Man Mooney, a used car salesman who employs Sweetums as a jack.  
*   Elliott Gould as the Compère who announces Miss Piggy as the winner of the Bogen County Beauty Pageant.  
*   Edgar Bergen as himself and Charlie McCarthy playing judges at the County Fair. This appearance marks Bergen's last film; he died soon after. The film was dedicated in his memory.  
*   Bob Hope as an Ice Cream Vendor serving cones to Fozzie at the County Fair.  
*   Richard Pryor as a Balloon Vendor selling balloons to Gonzo at the County Fair.  
*   Steve Martin as an insolent waiter working at the restaurant where Rowlf plays piano.  
*   Mel Brooks as Professor Krassman, a mad scientist hired by Doc Hopper.  
*   Cloris Leachman as Miss Tracy, Lew Lord's secretary who is allergic to animals.  
*   Orson Welles as Lew Lord, a Hollywood producer and studio executive. The character's name alludes to Sir Lew Grade, head of ATV, the British company that co-produced _The Muppet Show_.

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
After the popularity of the Muppets had grown following the success of _The Muppet Show_, Lew Grade agreed to finance the production of the film and signed the deal with his company ITC Entertainment,[[10]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199472-11) which helped Jim Henson finance the film.[[11]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-12) After the film's production greenlit, Jim Henson and selected team members traveled to California various times to develop the script, music,

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
and infrastructure in Hollywood to shoot the film.[[12]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-:6-13)James Frawley was hired to direct the movie due to the film's challenges.[[12]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-:6-13)

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
During Frawley and Henson's first meeting in London, they were concerned that the Muppets would not blend well in real life.[[13]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-Frawley-14)[[14]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-:5-15) Along with Frank Oz and the team,
they filmed and tested how the characters would appear in real-world locations during the first few days of June 1978 in a UK

A television monitor showed what was ahead.[[28]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199474-29)[[9]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-:22-10)

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
The closing reprise of "Rainbow Connection" featured a crowd of more than 250 Muppet characters—virtually every Muppet that had been created up to that point in time.[[9]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-:22-10)[[14]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-:5-15)[[29]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-:3-30) According to Henson Archivist Karen Falk,

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
137 puppeteers were enlisted from the Puppeteers of America (along with the regular Muppets performers) to perform every Muppet extant.[[9]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-:22-10)[[29]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-:3-30) Prior to the day-long filming of the shot, Henson gave the enthusiastic participants a lesson in the art of cinematic puppetry.

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
The scene involved 150 puppeteers performing in a pit that was 6 feet (1.8 m) deep and 17 feet (5.2 m) wide.[[9]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-:22-10)[[29]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-:3-30) In September 1978, Edgar Bergen, Henson's idol who appeared in a cameo role, died shortly after completing his scenes. Henson was asked by his family to say a few words with Kermit for his memorial service.

### Special guest stars (in order of appearance)
Henson agreed, and he attended Bergen's memorial service for its speech.[[30]](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaQHrOzAVQD3hZMpNCWnzIxEpkKbUnmzHF90pgx_hDs8JuTyh-MXzP0kebU_LMtDNU7PjE9T9gjstvGkZcybU0300wwXx8XueOSfuCmi-QRVc8OUkZSgGJ_EXU6hrt43kewlE0EjCZa_rBg#cite_note-FOOTNOTEDurrett199475-31) Henson dedicated the film to his memory.
The film's music and lyrics were written by Paul Williams and Kenneth Ascher. Regarding the music's composition, Williams said; "Jim Henson gave you more [creative] freedom than anybody I've ever worked with in my life. I said, 'You want to hear the songs as we're writing them?' He said, 'No. I'll hear them in the studio.

Title: It’s The Muppet Movie! With Our Very Special Guest Stars… – Perisphere
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
| Dan Howard |
The Muppet Movie _plays in stunning 4K at the Trylon Cinema from Sunday, August 2nd, through Tuesday, August 4th. For tickets, showtimes, and other series information, visit trylon.org._
* * *
Dom DeLuise,James Coburn,Madeline Khan,Telly Savalas,Carol Kane,Paul Williams,Milton Berle,Elliot Gould,Edgar Bergen (and Charlie), Bob Hope,Richard Pryor,Steve Martin,Mel Brooks,Cloris Lechman, and Orson Welles!
Talk about an all-star lineup of cameos, right? Jim Henson, director James Frawley, and writers Jerry Juhl and Jack Burns certainly pulled no punches with the Muppets’ silver screen debut. These days, I don’t think any of us could imagine a world without the Muppets, _The Muppet Movie_, or even “The Rainbow Connection.” However, the deeper connections that all these guest stars throughout _The Muppet Movie_ have to the Muppets themselves is something I absolutely can imagine.
As the Muppets gather in a Hollywood screening room for the first viewing of their motion picture debut, we see the origins of the ever-iconic Kermit the Frog (Jim Henson), Fozzy Bear (Frank Oz), The Great Gonzo (Dave Goelz), Ms. Piggy (Frank Oz), and all your favorite Muppets as they journey across America towards Hollywood, chasing their dreams of the spotlight, all while evading the crazy Doc Hopper (Charles Durning) and his assistant Max (Austin Pendleton) who is oddly obsessed with attaining Kermit as his mascot for his French-Fried Frog Legs restaurant franchise.
Now, I’d like to note: This article is purely speculative as we discuss folks like Elliot Gould, Richard Pryor, and Orson Welles, leaving these thoughts about their deeper connections to these characters of plush and fabric entirely to our imagination
To quote one of the greatest poets and songwriters of our time, Tom Waits, from his 2004 Harp Magazine ( http://tomwaitslibrary.info/biography/quotes/computers/ ) interview:

“We have a deficit of wonder. I think it’s because of computers. When I ask people questions now, they get on their computer—‘Gimme a few minutes and I’ll let ya know …’ And I’m like, ‘Noooooo!’ I want ’em to wonder about it, man! I don’t wanna know the answer—I just want ’em to wonder about it.”
I like to think Jim Henson himself would greatly approve, even encourage, this speculation and anything embodying the spirit of wonder.
Now, the majority, if not all, of the special guests in _The Muppet Movie_ had met Jim Henson on the talk show TV circuit, variety shows, and on _Saturday Night Live_ in the 70s and many of them (DeLuise, Martin, Pryor,Khan,Williams,Berle,Bergen, and Lechman) had their stints as guest hosting _The Muppet Show_ in seasons 2 and 5. The truth is, all actors are grown children at heart who love playing pretend and one of Jim Henson’s greatest gifts was reminding us of our inner child. Yet, it’s the ones whose first Muppet experience was being in _The Muppet Movie_ that intrigues me the most.
The first being the great Carol Kane, who famously plays the woman with a lisp who appears whenever Kermit repeats the word “Myth! Myth!” Responding with “Yeth?” Growing up, her mother, Joy, was a jazz singer, teacher, dancer and pianist and her father was an architect. The talents from her mother and the art of building your work from her father were no doubt a recipe for success! After she appeared with Jack Nicholson in such revered films as _Carnal Knowledge_ and _Dog Day Afternoon_, Carol would gravitate towards comedy following her _Muppet Movie_ casting. Perhaps Carol had that reawakening of her own inner child after sharing her debut scene with a talking lime-green frog? Perhaps even awakening her inner frog? Judging by her performances in _The Princess Bride_ and _Addams Family Values_, “Myth” Kane naturally inhabits that goofball Henson-Muppet energy.

Speaking of goofball energy, let’s talk about the now-hundred-year-old comedy legend: Mel Brooks. With films like _The Producers, Blazing Saddles_, and _Young Frankenstein_, the guy was already a bit of a Muppet in his own right. His cameo as Professor Krassman, it seemed to provide a slightly different outlet for his style of comedy. Brooks admitted that a lot of his comedy may have been rooted in anger and hostility due to his father dying of tuberculosis as age 34. Brooks, at the time, was only 2 years old.
“There’s an outrage there. I may be angry at God, or at the world, for that. And I’m sure a lot of my comedy is based on anger and hostility. Growing up in Williamsburg, I learned to clothe it in comedy to spare myself problems—like a punch in the face.” – Mel Brooks, Live at the Geffen
Brooks was also drafted into the US Army at age 18, fighting in the Battle of the Bulge. Speaking about his experience, Brooks would recall, “Along the roadside, you’d see bodies wrapped up in mattress covers and stacked in a ditch, and those would be Americans, that could be me. I sang all the time… I never wanted to think about it… .” So, when he was offered a part in The Muppet Movie, it feels like it offered Brooks a chance to channel his comedic talents through joy instead of rage. Maybe realizing that he would be a part of a movie that kids would fall in love with, like he did with _Anything Goes_ at age 9, he knew he could be showing the next generation the path to their own dreams, reminding himself why he wanted to be on stage and the silver screen.

Regarding big-screen stars, Elliott Gould’s cameo intrigues me the most. In the ‘70s, Gould was an immaculate star in pop culture. With roles in films like _M*A*S*H_ and _The Long Goodbye_, and having been married to Barbara Streisand, he was top of the world. However, Gould must have needed a break from the dramas and serious films. Even though he had been in a musical comedy beforehand, Williams Friedkin’s _The Night They Raided Minsky’s_, he likely needed to let loose a bit. I do wonder if Jim Henson knew about Gould’s parents’ professions prior to casting him. Gould’s mother sold artificial flowers to beauty shops, and his father was a textiles buyer in the garment business. His family clearly knew about beautiful things, and having Gould play a beauty pageant judge, crowning Miss Piggy the winner, feels like a fantastic, personal full circle moment. Perhaps, in his own unique way, it took him back to his own childhood. All that and finding his way back to musical comedy? The Muppets and Elliott Gould sure were a match made in heaven! Gould even returned to the Muppet world 5 years later, appearing as a cop in _The Muppets Take Manhattan_.

texts.3:
The film stars Muppet performers Henson, Frank Oz, Jerry Nelson, Richard Hunt, and Dave Goelz, as well as Charles Durning and Austin Pendleton, and it features cameo appearances by Bob Hope, Dom DeLuise, James Coburn, Cloris Leachman, Richard Pryor, Telly Savalas, Edgar Bergen (in his final film appearance before his death), Orson Welles, Madeline Kahn, Milton Berle, Carol Kane, Steve Martin, Mel Brooks, Elliott Gould, and Paul Williams. Notable for its surreal humour, meta-references and prolific use of cameos, _The Muppet Movie_ was released by Associated Film Distribution in the United Kingdom on May 31, 1979, and in the United States on June 22, 1979.
The film received critical praise, including two Academy Award nominations for Paul Williams and Kenneth Ascher's musical score and their song "Rainbow Connection". The film grossed $76.7 million worldwide against an $8 million budget. _The Muppet Movie_ was followed by seven feature films starring the Muppets as well as several more television series and media. In 2009, the film was deemed "culturally, historically, or aesthetically significant" by the Library of Congress and selected for preservation in the National Film Registry.
The story opens with the Muppets sitting down for a private screening of a movie that acts as an origin story of how they all met.
Kermit the Frog lives a simple life in a Florida swamp. After he plays his banjo and sings "Rainbow Connection", he is approached by Bernie, a talent agent who encourages him to pursue a career in show business. Inspired, Kermit sets off on a cross-country trip to Hollywood.
texts.4:
He meets Fozzie Bear, who is working as a hapless stand-up comedian, and invites him on his journey. The two set out in Fozzie's 1951 Studebaker but are pursued by entrepreneur Doc Hopper and his assistant Max, who try to convince Kermit to be the new spokesfrog of Hopper's struggling French-friedfrog legs restaurant franchise. Horrified, Kermit refuses, and he and Fozzie drive away. Unwilling to accept Kermit's refusal, Hopper follows the pair and resorts to increasingly forceful means of persuasion. In an old church, Kermit and Fozzie meet the rock band Dr. Teeth and the Electric Mayhem, and their manager Scooter, who help them disguise their car. Driving on, they meet and are joined by Gonzo and his girlfriend Camilla the Chicken, who are also interested in becoming movie stars. They trade in their failing vehicle at a used car lot, where they meet Sweetums. They invite Sweetums to come with them, but he runs away. The others drive away, only for Sweetums to emerge and reveal that he had only gone to pack his things.
The group meets Miss Piggy at a county fair and she and Kermit become love-stricken with each other. When they meet for dinner that night, Hopper and Max abduct Miss Piggy as bait to lure Kermit. When they capture Kermit, Hopper orders mad scientist Professor Krassman to give Kermit an electric lobotomy so that he would willingly perform in Hopper's advertisements, but Miss Piggy knocks out Hopper's henchmen and causes Krassman to have his brain fried by his own device. Immediately after the fight, however, Miss Piggy receives a job offer and abandons a devastated Kermit.
texts.5:
Joined by Rowlf the Dog, the Muppets pick up Miss Piggy – who is hitchhiking on the side of the road – and continue their journey; but their car breaks down in the desert. Sitting at a campfire, the group realizes that they will likely miss the auditions the next day. Kermit wanders off, ashamed for bringing his friends on a fruitless journey, but personal reflection restores his commitment. He returns to camp, where he discovers that the Electric Mayhem have come to their rescue, having learned of their plight by reading ahead in the film's script. The Mayhem offer to drive the group the rest of the way in their bus.
The group is warned by a reformed Max that Hopper has hired an assassin, Snake Walker, to kill Kermit. Kermit decides to face his aggressor and proposes a Western-style showdown in a nearby ghost town. There, they find inventor Dr. Bunsen Honeydew and his assistant Beaker. Kermit and his friends are saved when one of Dr. Honeydew's inventions, "insta-grow" pills, enlarges Mayhem drummer Animal, who frightens away Hopper and his henchmen.
Once the Muppets reach the Hollywood studio, they meet executive Lew Lord, who signs them to a "standard 'rich and famous' contract". The first take in their attempt to perform the script goes awry when Gonzo crashes into the prop rainbow, which knocks the scenery down and an explosion blows a hole in the roof of the studio, but a real rainbow shines through the hole and illuminates all the Muppets. Joined by characters from other Henson productions – including _Sesame Street_, _[Emmet Otter's Jug-Band Christmas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmet\_Otter's\_Jug-Band\_Christmas "Emmet Otter's Jug-Band Christmas")_, and _The Land of Gorch_ – the Muppets sing the final verse in a reprise of "Rainbow Connection". As the film ends, Sweetums tears through the screen, elated that he caught up with them.

| Dan Howard |
The Muppet Movie _plays in stunning 4K at the Trylon Cinema from Sunday, August 2nd, through Tuesday, August 4th. For tickets, showtimes, and other series information, visit trylon.org._
* * *
Dom DeLuise,James Coburn,Madeline Khan,Telly Savalas,Carol Kane,Paul Williams,Milton Berle,Elliot Gould,Edgar Bergen (and Charlie), Bob Hope,Richard Pryor,Steve Martin,Mel Brooks,Cloris Lechman, and Orson Welles!
Talk about an all-star lineup of cameos, right? Jim Henson, director James Frawley, and writers Jerry Juhl and Jack Burns certainly pulled no punches with the Muppets’ silver screen debut. These days, I don’t think any of us could imagine a world without the Muppets, _The Muppet Movie_, or even “The Rainbow Connection.” However, the deeper connections that all these guest stars throughout _The Muppet Movie_ have to the Muppets themselves is something I absolutely can imagine.
As the Muppets gather in a Hollywood screening room for the first viewing of their motion picture debut, we see the origins of the ever-iconic Kermit the Frog (Jim Henson), Fozzy Bear (Frank Oz), The Great Gonzo (Dave Goelz), Ms. Piggy (Frank Oz), and all your favorite Muppets as they journey across America towards Hollywood, chasing their dreams of the spotlight, all while evading the crazy Doc Hopper (Charles Durning) and his assistant Max (Austin Pendleton) who is oddly obsessed with attaining Kermit as his mascot for his French-Fried Frog Legs restaurant franchise.
Now, I’d like to note: This article is purely speculative as we discuss folks like Elliot Gould, Richard Pryor, and Orson Welles, leaving these thoughts about their deeper connections to these characters of plush and fabric entirely to our imagination
To quote one of the greatest poets and songwriters of our time, Tom Waits, from his 2004 Harp Magazine ( http://tomwaitslibrary.info/biography/quotes/computers/ ) interview:
texts.1:
“We have a deficit of wonder. I think it’s because of computers. When I ask people questions now, they get on their computer—‘Gimme a few minutes and I’ll let ya know …’ And I’m like, ‘Noooooo!’ I want ’em to wonder about it, man! I don’t wanna know the answer—I just want ’em to wonder about it.”
I like to think Jim Henson himself would greatly approve, even encourage, this speculation and anything embodying the spirit of wonder.
Now, the majority, if not all, of the special guests in _The Muppet Movie_ had met Jim Henson on the talk show TV circuit, variety shows, and on _Saturday Night Live_ in the 70s and many of them (DeLuise, Martin, Pryor,Khan,Williams,Berle,Bergen, and Lechman) had their stints as guest hosting _The Muppet Show_ in seasons 2 and 5. The truth is, all actors are grown children at heart who love playing pretend and one of Jim Henson’s greatest gifts was reminding us of our inner child. Yet, it’s the ones whose first Muppet experience was being in _The Muppet Movie_ that intrigues me the most.
The first being the great Carol Kane, who famously plays the woman with a lisp who appears whenever Kermit repeats the word “Myth! Myth!” Responding with “Yeth?” Growing up, her mother, Joy, was a jazz singer, teacher, dancer and pianist and her father was an architect. The talents from her mother and the art of building your work from her father were no doubt a recipe for success! After she appeared with Jack Nicholson in such revered films as _Carnal Knowledge_ and _Dog Day Afternoon_, Carol would gravitate towards comedy following her _Muppet Movie_ casting. Perhaps Carol had that reawakening of her own inner child after sharing her debut scene with a talking lime-green frog? Perhaps even awakening her inner frog? Judging by her performances in _The Princess Bride_ and _Addams Family Values_, “Myth” Kane naturally inhabits that goofball Henson-Muppet energy.
texts.2:
Speaking of goofball energy, let’s talk about the now-hundred-year-old comedy legend: Mel Brooks. With films like _The Producers, Blazing Saddles_, and _Young Frankenstein_, the guy was already a bit of a Muppet in his own right. His cameo as Professor Krassman, it seemed to provide a slightly different outlet for his style of comedy. Brooks admitted that a lot of his comedy may have been rooted in anger and hostility due to his father dying of tuberculosis as age 34. Brooks, at the time, was only 2 years old.
“There’s an outrage there. I may be angry at God, or at the world, for that. And I’m sure a lot of my comedy is based on anger and hostility. Growing up in Williamsburg, I learned to clothe it in comedy to spare myself problems—like a punch in the face.” – Mel Brooks, Live at the Geffen
Brooks was also drafted into the US Army at age 18, fighting in the Battle of the Bulge. Speaking about his experience, Brooks would recall, “Along the roadside, you’d see bodies wrapped up in mattress covers and stacked in a ditch, and those would be Americans, that could be me. I sang all the time… I never wanted to think about it… .” So, when he was offered a part in The Muppet Movie, it feels like it offered Brooks a chance to channel his comedic talents through joy instead of rage. Maybe realizing that he would be a part of a movie that kids would fall in love with, like he did with _Anything Goes_ at age 9, he knew he could be showing the next generation the path to their own dreams, reminding himself why he wanted to be on stage and the silver screen.
texts.3: Regarding big-screen stars, Elliott Gould’s cameo intrigues me the most. In the ‘70s, Gould was an immaculate star in pop culture. With roles in films like _M*A*S*H_ and _The Long Goodbye_, and having been married to Barbara Streisand, he was top of the world. However, Gould must have needed a break from the dramas and serious films. Even though he had been in a musical comedy beforehand, Williams Friedkin’s _The Night They Raided Minsky’s_, he likely needed to let loose a bit. I do wonder if Jim Henson knew about Gould’s parents’ professions prior to casting him. Gould’s mother sold artificial flowers to beauty shops, and his father was a textiles buyer in the garment business. His family clearly knew about beautiful things, and having Gould play a beauty pageant judge, crowning Miss Piggy the winner, feels like a fantastic, personal full circle moment. Perhaps, in his own unique way, it took him back to his own childhood. All that and finding his way back to musical comedy? The Muppets and Elliott Gould sure were a match made in heaven! Gould even returned to the Muppet world 5 years later, appearing as a cop in _The Muppets Take Manhattan_.

# Bob Hope
Leslie Townes “Bob” Hope (born in London, England, May 29, 1903, died July 27, 2003)is one of the most popular comedians of American movies and television. He started in vaudeville and radio, then Paramount cast him in _The Big Broadcast of 1938_ with W. C. Fields, _The Cat and the Canary_(1939) with Paulette Goddard, _My Favorite Brunette_(1947) with Dorothy Lamour, _The Pale Face_ (1948) with Jane Russell, and a series of “road” movies with Bing Crosby from 1940 to 1962.
Read **_Ready for My deMille: Profiles in Excellence – Bob Hope, 1963_**by Philip Berk

Title: List of awards and nominations received by Bob Hope
